Exploratory Data Analysis¶

Univariate analysis¶

In [57]:
# function to plot a boxplot and a histogram along the same scale.


def histogram_boxplot(df, feature, figsize=(12, 7), kde=False, bins=None):
    """
    Boxplot and histogram combined

    data: dataframe
    feature: dataframe column
    figsize: size of figure (default (12,7))
    kde: whether to the show density curve (default False)
    bins: number of bins for histogram (default None)
    """
    f2, (ax_box2, ax_hist2) = plt.subplots(
        nrows=2,  # Number of rows of the subplot grid= 2
        sharex=True,  # x-axis will be shared among all subplots
        gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": (0.25, 0.75)},
        figsize=figsize,
    )  # creating the 2 subplots
    sns.boxplot(
        data=df, x=feature, ax=ax_box2, showmeans=True, color="violet"
    )  # boxplot will be created and a star will indicate the mean value of the column
    sns.histplot(
        data=df, x=feature, kde=kde, ax=ax_hist2, bins=bins, palette="winter"
    ) if bins else sns.histplot(
        data=df, x=feature, kde=kde, ax=ax_hist2
    )  # For histogram
    ax_hist2.axvline(
        df[feature].mean(), color="green", linestyle="--"
    )  # Add mean to the histogram
    ax_hist2.axvline(
        df[feature].median(), color="black", linestyle="-"
    )  # Add median to the histogram
In [58]:
# function to create labeled barplots


def labeled_barplot(data, feature, perc=False, n=None):
    """
    Barplot with percentage at the top

    data: dataframe
    feature: dataframe column
    perc: whether to display percentages instead of count (default is False)
    n: displays the top n category levels (default is None, i.e., display all levels)
    """

    total = len(data[feature])  # length of the column
    count = data[feature].nunique()
    if n is None:
        plt.figure(figsize=(count + 1, 5))
    else:
        plt.figure(figsize=(n + 1, 5))

    plt.xticks(rotation=90, fontsize=15)
    ax = sns.countplot(
        data=data,
        x=feature,
        order=data[feature].value_counts().index[:n].sort_values(),
    )

    for p in ax.patches:
        if perc == True:
            label = "{:.1f}%".format(
                100 * p.get_height() / total
            )  # percentage of each class of the category
        else:
            label = p.get_height()  # count of each level of the category

        x = p.get_x() + p.get_width() / 2  # width of the plot
        y = p.get_height()  # height of the plot

        ax.annotate(
            label,
            (x, y),
            ha="center",
            va="center",
            size=12,
            xytext=(0, 5),
            textcoords="offset points",
        )  # annotate the percentage

    plt.show()  # show the plot

Current Price¶

In [59]:
histogram_boxplot(df, 'Current Price')

Based on the histogram and boxplot for Current Price, the following observations can be made:¶

Distribution Shape: The distribution of Current Price is highly right-skewed, with the majority of stocks concentrated at lower price levels and a long tail extending toward significantly higher prices. This indicates that while most companies in the dataset trade at relatively modest prices, a small number of stocks command exceptionally high valuations that distort the overall distribution.¶
Central Tendency: The median (black dashed line) is considerably lower than the mean (green dashed line), further confirming the right-skewed nature of the distribution. This suggests that the majority of companies have relatively low current prices.¶
Spread and Outliers: The boxplot reveals a large number of outliers on the upper end of the price spectrum, confirming that while most stocks fall within a typical and relatively narrow price range, a handful of companies have exceptionally high current prices that pull the mean upward and widen the overall spread.¶

Price Change¶

In [60]:
histogram_boxplot(df, 'Price Change')

Based on the histogram and boxplot for Price Change, the following observations can be made:¶

Distribution Shape: The distribution of Price Change appears roughly symmetrical and bell-shaped, centered around zero. This suggests that positive and negative price changes occur with broadly similar frequencies across the dataset, with the majority of stocks recording modest changes close to zero over the observed period.¶
Central Tendency: The mean (green dashed line) and median (black dashed line) are very close to each other, and both sit near zero, indicating that, on average, stocks did not experience a significant net price change over the observed period.¶
Spread and Outliers: The boxplot reveals that while most price changes are clustered tightly around the center, several outliers are present on both the positive and negative ends of the distribution. These outliers represent stocks that experienced unusually large gains or losses, which may be attributable to significant company-specific events, broader market movements, or sector-level volatility.¶

Volatility¶

In [61]:
histogram_boxplot(df, 'Volatility')

Based on the histogram and boxplot for Volatility, the following observations can be made:¶

Distribution Shape: The distribution of Volatility is moderately right-skewed, with the bulk of stocks concentrated at the lower end of the volatility spectrum and a long tail extending toward higher values. The majority of stocks record a volatility score between 1.0 and 1.7, representing the typical risk level within this dataset, while a smaller segment exhibits significantly higher price fluctuations.¶
Central Tendency: The mean (green dashed line) is slightly higher than the median (black solid line), which is consistent with the right-skewed nature of the distribution. This divergence indicates that a small number of highly volatile stocks are pulling the average upward, making the median a more representative measure of the typical volatility level across the dataset.¶
Spread and Outliers: The boxplot reveals numerous outliers on the upper end of the volatility scale, with the highest observed volatility exceeding 4.5. These outliers represent a distinct segment of stocks with exceptionally high price fluctuations, which may be attributable to elevated risk profiles, company-specific events, or particular market conditions affecting these assets. Their presence warrants careful consideration during modeling, as they have the potential to disproportionately influence model performance if left unaddressed.¶

ROE¶

In [62]:
histogram_boxplot(df, 'ROE')

Based on the histogram and boxplot for ROE (Return on Equity), the following observations can be made:¶

Distribution Shape: The distribution of ROE is the most heavily right-skewed feature encountered in this dataset so far, with an extreme concentration of values at the lower end and a very long tail extending toward exceptionally high values. This indicates that the vast majority of companies record relatively modest returns on equity, while a small number of companies exhibit extraordinarily high ROE figures that severely distort the overall distribution.¶
Central Tendency: The median (black solid line) is considerably lower than the mean (green dashed line), reinforcing the extreme right-skewness of the distribution. This substantial divergence between the two measures of central tendency confirms that the mean is being dragged drastically upward by a small number of extremely high-value outliers, making the median a far more reliable representation of the typical ROE level across the dataset.¶
Spread and Outliers: The boxplot reveals a massive concentration of outliers on the upper end of the ROE spectrum, extending as far as 917 — the highest value observed across all features analyzed thus far. These outliers likely represent companies with extraordinarily high profitability, very low or near-zero equity bases, or specific accounting practices that inflate the ROE figure. If left unaddressed, these extreme values have the potential to significantly distort clustering results and model performance, and should therefore be treated — through capping, log transformation, or robust scaling — prior to any further analysis or modeling.¶

Cash Ratio¶

In [63]:
histogram_boxplot(df, 'Cash Ratio')

Based on the histogram and boxplot for Cash Ratio, the following observations can be made:¶

Distribution Shape: The distribution of Cash Ratio continues the trend of strong right-skewness observed across several other financial metrics in this dataset. The vast majority of companies maintain a low cash ratio, with a massive concentration of values in the lowest bin, while a long tail extends toward exceptionally high values. This indicates that while most companies operate with modest cash reserves relative to their liabilities, a small number maintain extraordinarily high liquidity positions that severely distort the overall distribution.¶
Central Tendency: The median (black solid line) is significantly lower than the mean (green dashed line), which is characteristic of a heavily right-skewed distribution. This substantial divergence confirms that the mean is being pulled considerably upward by a small number of extremely high-value outliers, making the median a far more reliable representation of the typical cash ratio level across the dataset.¶
Spread and Outliers: The boxplot reveals numerous outliers on the upper end of the Cash Ratio spectrum, beginning from approximately 200 and extending to a maximum of nearly 958 — more than twenty times the median value. These extreme outliers represent companies sitting on disproportionately large cash reserves relative to their liabilities, likely reflecting an exceptionally conservative financial strategy, recent large-scale asset disposals, or specific liquidity management practices.¶

Net Cash Flow¶

In [64]:
histogram_boxplot(df, 'Net Cash Flow')

Based on the histogram and boxplot for Net Cash Flow, the following observations can be made:¶

Distribution Shape: Unlike the heavily right-skewed distributions observed across several other financial metrics in this dataset, the Net Cash Flow distribution exhibits a distinctly different pattern — characterized by an exceptionally tall and narrow peak centered around zero, with extreme tails extending in both directions. The vast majority of companies record a net cash flow very close to zero, while a small number of companies operate on a dramatically different financial scale, generating or consuming cash flows in the tens of billions.¶
Central Tendency: The mean (green dashed line) and median (black solid line) are nearly identical and both centered around zero, indicating a roughly symmetric distribution for the core data. This close alignment between the two measures of central tendency is notable, as it contrasts sharply with the heavily skewed distributions observed in features such as ROE and Cash Ratio. However, while the central tendency measures suggest symmetry, they do not fully capture the extreme variability present at both ends of the distribution, and should therefore be interpreted alongside the spread and outlier analysis below.¶
Spread and Outliers: The boxplot reveals a significant number of outliers in both directions. Some companies record massive negative net cash flows as low as -1.12 × 10¹⁰, while others record massive positive net cash flows as high as 2.07 × 10¹⁰ — a scale of tens of billions of dollars. These extreme values likely represent large corporations engaged in significant capital investments, major divestitures, substantial debt financing activities, or exceptional operating performance. The presence of outliers on both ends confirms that while most companies manage their cash flows within a relatively tight range, a small number of financial giants in the dataset are operating on an entirely different scale.¶

Net Income¶

histogram_boxplot(df, 'Net Income')

Based on the histogram and boxplot for Net Income, the following observations can be made:¶

Distribution Shape: The distribution of Net Income closely mirrors that of Net Cash Flow, exhibiting a sharply concentrated peak near zero with extreme tails extending in both directions. The vast majority of companies record net income figures clustered tightly around zero, reflecting modest profitability for the typical company in the dataset. However, the distribution spans a wide range — from approximately -24 billion to +24 billion — confirming the presence of both heavily loss-making companies and exceptionally profitable corporations operating on a dramatically larger financial scale than the majority.¶
Central Tendency: The median (black solid line) sits close to the peak of the distribution, representing the performance of the typical company in the dataset. The mean (green dashed line), however, is pulled noticeably to the right by high-performing positive outliers, creating a divergence between the two measures of central tendency. While both measures are broadly positive and near zero, neither fully captures the extent of variability present at the extremes of the distribution, and should therefore be interpreted in conjunction with the spread and outlier analysis below.¶
Spread and Outliers: The boxplot reveals extreme outliers at both ends of the spectrum. On the negative end, some companies record losses as severe as approximately -2.4 × 10¹⁰, representing businesses experiencing significant financial distress, heavy write-offs, or substantial operating losses. On the positive end, certain highly profitable corporations record net income figures exceeding +2.4 × 10¹⁰, reflecting strong market performance, favorable industry dynamics, or exceptional profitability driven by scale advantages. These extreme values confirm that while most companies in the dataset operate within a relatively modest income range, a small number of financial giants sit at the far ends of the distribution.¶

histogram_boxplot(df, 'Earnings Per Share')

Based on the histogram and boxplot for Earnings Per Share (EPS), the following observations can be made:¶

Distribution Shape: The distribution of EPS exhibits a relatively symmetric and narrow concentration of values around the median, with the bulk of companies recording earnings per share clustered within a modest range. However, despite this central symmetry, extreme outliers on both the positive and negative ends create considerable variance across the full distribution — a pattern that distinguishes EPS from the heavily right-skewed features analyzed earlier in this dataset.¶
Central Tendency: The mean (green dashed line) and median (black solid line) are nearly identical, both sitting close to approximately $2.90, indicating that the central data is fairly balanced and that the typical company in the dataset records a modest but positive earnings per share. The close alignment between the two measures of central tendency confirms the approximate symmetry of the core distribution, though this symmetry should not be interpreted as an absence of variability, given the presence of extreme outliers at both ends.¶
Spread and Outliers: The boxplot reveals significant outliers on both ends of the EPS spectrum. On the negative end, several companies record substantial losses per share, with the most extreme, likely reflecting businesses experiencing severe financial distress, significant write-offs, or exceptional one-time losses. On the positive end, high-performing stocks reach EPS values as high as approximately $50, representing companies with exceptionally strong profitability, favorable industry positioning, or specific one-time gains. The presence of extreme outliers in both directions contributes to high overall variance in this feature and warrants careful consideration during preprocessing.¶

Based on the histogram and boxplot for Estimated Shares Outstanding, the following observations can be made:¶

Distribution Shape: The distribution of Estimated Shares Outstanding is heavily right-skewed, continuing the pattern of extreme skewness observed across several other financial metrics in this dataset. The vast majority of companies have a relatively modest number of shares outstanding, with values concentrated tightly at the lower end of the distribution. A long tail extends toward extraordinarily high values, reflecting the presence of a small number of large corporations whose share counts dwarf those of the typical company in the dataset. It is worth noting that the x-axis scale is expressed in billions (1e9), underscoring the massive disparity in scale between mid-sized firms and the largest market players.¶
Central Tendency: The median (black solid line) is significantly lower than the mean (green dashed line), which is characteristic of a heavily right-skewed distribution. This substantial divergence confirms that the mean is being pulled considerably upward by a small number of mega-cap companies with an enormous number of shares outstanding, making the median a far more reliable representation of the typical share count across the dataset.¶
Spread and Outliers: The boxplot reveals a significant concentration of outliers on the upper end of the Estimated Shares Outstanding spectrum, with some companies exceeding 6 × 10⁹ (6 billion) shares outstanding — a figure that confirms the extreme disparity between the largest and most typical companies in the dataset. These outliers likely represent very large market capitalization corporations with complex capital structures, a long history of share issuance, or specific corporate governance arrangements that result in exceptionally high share counts. Their presence introduces considerable variance into this feature and warrants careful treatment prior to clustering.¶

A long tail extends toward much higher values, reflecting a smaller segment of stocks with exceptionally elevated valuations. This pattern confirms that while most companies in the dataset trade at conventional earnings multiples, a distinct group of high-valuation stocks sits well beyond the typical range.¶

The mean is being pulled considerably upward by a small number of companies with extremely high P/E ratios, making it an unreliable measure of typical valuation in this dataset. The median, therefore, provides a far more representative indication of the valuation level of the typical stock in the sample.¶
Spread and Outliers: The boxplot reveals a substantial number of outliers beyond the upper whisker, with some extreme values exceeding a P/E ratio of 100, and the most extreme observation reaching over 528. Distribution Shape: Unlike the heavily right-skewed distributions observed across most other financial metrics in this dataset, the P/B Ratio exhibits a relatively symmetric central mass, with the highest frequency of values clustered tightly in the -10 to 10 range and the sharpest concentration occurring around zero. However, this apparent central symmetry is significantly disrupted by extreme outliers at both ends of the distribution, which introduce considerable variance and make the overall distribution more complex to interpret and handle than its central tendency alone would suggest.¶

This close alignment reflects the approximate symmetry of the core distribution and confirms that the typical company in the dataset has a P/B Ratio hovering around zero — indicating that market value and book value are broadly comparable for most stocks. However, as with Net Cash Flow and EPS, the near-identical mean and median should not be interpreted as an absence of variability, given the presence of extreme outliers at both ends that significantly widen the overall spread.¶

# function to create labeled barplots


def labeled_barplot(df, feature, perc=False, n=None):
    """
    Barplot with percentage at the top

    data: dataframe
    feature: dataframe column
    perc: whether to display percentages instead of count (default is False)
    n: displays the top n category levels (default is None, i.e., display all levels)
    """

    total = len(df[feature])  # length of the column
    count = df[feature].nunique()
    if n is None:
        plt.figure(figsize=(count + 1, 5))
    else:
        plt.figure(figsize=(n + 1, 5))

    plt.xticks(rotation=90, fontsize=15)
    ax = sns.countplot(
        data=df,
        x=feature,
        order=df[feature].value_counts().index[:n].sort_values(),
    )

    for p in ax.patches:
        if perc == True:
            label = "{:.1f}%".format(
                100 * p.get_height() / total
            )  # percentage of each class of the category
        else:
            label = p.get_height()  # count of each level of the category

        x = p.get_x() + p.get_width() / 2  # width of the plot
        y = p.get_height()  # height of the plot

        ax.annotate(
            label,
            (x, y),
            ha="center",
            va="center",
            size=12,
            xytext=(0, 5),
            textcoords="offset points",
        )  # annotate the percentage

    plt.show()  # show the plot

Bivariate Analysis¶

Based on the correlation heatmap, the following observations can be made:¶

Positive Correlations:¶

Net Income & Estimated Shares Outstanding (0.59): The strongest positive correlation in the dataset exists between Net Income and Estimated Shares Outstanding, suggesting that larger companies — as measured by the volume of shares issued — tend to report higher absolute net income figures.¶
Net Income & Earnings Per Share (0.56): A strong positive relationship exists between total net income and earnings per share, which is broadly expected — higher overall profitability generally translates into higher earnings on a per-share basis,¶
Current Price & Earnings Per Share (0.48): A moderate positive relationship between current stock price and earnings per share suggests that stocks with higher per-share earnings tend to command higher market prices. This is consistent with fundamental valuation theory, whereby stronger earnings performance is typically rewarded with higher market valuations.¶

Notable Negative Correlations:¶

Price Change & Volatility (-0.41): A moderate inverse relationship between price change and volatility suggests that stocks experiencing stronger price appreciation tend to exhibit lower volatility, while highly volatile stocks may struggle to sustain consistent positive price movements.¶
ROE & Earnings Per Share (-0.41): An interesting and somewhat counterintuitive inverse relationship exists between Return on Equity and Earnings Per Share in this dataset. This may indicate that high-EPS stocks in this group tend to have larger equity bases, which dilutes the ROE percentage despite strong absolute earnings — a nuance worth bearing in mind when interpreting these two metrics independently during modeling.¶
Volatility & Net Income (-0.38): A moderate negative relationship between volatility and net income suggests that more profitable companies tend to exhibit lower stock price volatility.¶

Largely Independent Variables:¶

Net Cash Flow: This metric exhibits near-zero correlation with the majority of other variables in the dataset, with all correlation values falling between -0.05 and 0.11. This confirms that Net Cash Flow captures unique financial information that is not redundant with income or price metrics, and reinforces its value as an independent feature in the clustering model.¶
P/E and P/B Ratios: Both valuation ratios are largely uncorrelated with the other fundamental performance metrics in this dataset, suggesting that market-based valuation multiples move independently of the underlying operational and financial performance indicators captured by the remaining features.¶

Data Preprocessing¶

Outlier Check¶

Let's plot the boxplots of all numerical columns to check for outliers.¶

In [78]:
plt.figure(figsize=(15, 12))

numeric_columns = df.select_dtypes(include=np.number).columns.tolist()

for i, variable in enumerate(numeric_columns):
    plt.subplot(3, 4, i + 1)
    plt.boxplot(df[variable], whis=1.5)
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.title(variable)

plt.show()

Based on the boxplots of all numerical columns, the following observations can be made regarding the distribution and outlier characteristics of the features in this dataset:¶

Right-Skewed Features with High-End Outliers — Current Price, ROE, Cash Ratio, Estimated Shares Outstanding, and P/E Ratio: These five features share a common pattern of strong right-skewness, with numerous outliers concentrated on the upper end of their respective distributions. In each case, a small number of companies record exceptionally high values — whether in terms of stock price, return on equity, liquidity, share count, or earnings multiple — that pull the mean considerably above the median and introduce significant variance into the distribution. This pattern is characteristic of financial datasets where a handful of large, high-performing, or structurally unique companies dominate the upper tail while the majority of firms cluster at more modest levels.¶
Balanced Distribution with Notable Tail Outliers — Price Change: Price Change stands apart from the majority of features in this dataset by exhibiting a relatively symmetric and balanced distribution centered around zero. However, notable outliers are present at both ends of the spectrum, representing stocks that experienced either exceptionally large gains or steep losses during the observed period. While the central distribution is well-behaved, these tail observations warrant attention during preprocessing as they may reflect significant company-specific events or broader market disruptions.¶
Bidirectional Outliers — Net Cash Flow, Net Income, Earnings Per Share, and P/B Ratio: These four features exhibit outliers at both the negative and positive extremes, distinguishing them from the right-skewed features above. Negative outliers represent companies experiencing significant financial losses, heavily negative cash flows, or negative book equity — the latter being particularly relevant for P/B Ratio, where negative values arise from accumulated losses or aggressive share repurchase programmes. Positive outliers, on the other hand, represent highly profitable corporations, companies generating exceptional cash flows, or stocks commanding very high market-to-book premiums. The presence of extreme values in both directions introduces high variance and makes these features particularly sensitive to the choice of scaling technique prior to clustering.¶
Scale Disparity — Net Cash Flow, Net Income, and Estimated Shares Outstanding: Among all features in the dataset, Net Cash Flow, Net Income, and Estimated Shares Outstanding exhibit the most extreme scale disparities, with outlier values reaching into the tens of billions. This reflects the structural reality of financial datasets where a small number of large blue-chip corporations operate on a fundamentally different financial scale compared to the majority of mid-sized firms. If left unaddressed, these features risk dominating the distance calculations in the clustering model and rendering the contributions of other features effectively negligible.¶

Scaling¶

Let's scale the data before we proceed with clustering.¶

In [79]:

scaler = StandardScaler()

# Select only numerical columns for the subset
subset = df.select_dtypes(include=np.number)

subset_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(subset)

subset_scaled_df = pd.DataFrame(subset_scaled, columns=subset.columns)

K-means Clustering¶

Checking Elbow Plot¶

In [81]:
k_means_df = subset_scaled_df.copy()
In [82]:
clusters = range(1, 15)
meanDistortions = []

for k in clusters:
    model = KMeans(n_clusters=k, random_state=1)
    model.fit(subset_scaled_df)
    prediction = model.predict(k_means_df)
    distortion = (
        sum(np.min(cdist(k_means_df, model.cluster_centers_, "euclidean"), axis=1))
        / k_means_df.shape[0]
    )

    meanDistortions.append(distortion)

    print("Number of Clusters:", k, "\tAverage Distortion:", distortion)

plt.plot(clusters, meanDistortions, "bx-")
plt.xlabel("k")
plt.ylabel("Average Distortion")
plt.title("Selecting k with the Elbow Method", fontsize=20)
plt.show()

Based on the Elbow Method and Average Distortion plots, the following observations can be made regarding the optimal number of clusters for this dataset:¶

Decreasing Distortion: As the number of clusters k increases, the average distortion — measured as the sum of squared distances from each data point to its assigned cluster center — decreases consistently, as expected. This reflects the fundamental principle that adding more clusters always reduces the within-cluster variance, since each additional center is able to capture a more granular subset of the data.¶
Initial Significant Drops: The most pronounced reductions in distortion occur as k moves from 1 to 4, indicating that transitioning from a single group to four distinct clusters captures a substantial portion of the data's underlying structure. Each additional cluster in this range contributes meaningfully to reducing the average distance between data points and their assigned centers, confirming that the data contains at least four genuinely distinct groupings.¶
Identifying the Elbow: The distortion curve begins to level off noticeably after k = 4, with a secondary inflection point observable around k = 7. These two values represent the most defensible elbow points in the curve — the stages at which the marginal benefit of adding an additional cluster diminishes most clearly relative to the preceding reductions.¶
In [87]:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import time
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans

# 1. Define the range of clusters to test
clusters = range(1, 11)
distortions = []
fit_times = []

# 2. Calculate Distortion (Inertia) and Fit Time for each k
for k in clusters:
    model = KMeans(n_clusters=k, n_init=10, random_state=1)
    
    start_time = time.time()
    model.fit(k_means_df)
    end_time = time.time()
    
    distortions.append(model.inertia_)
    fit_times.append(end_time - start_time)

# 3. Plotting the results (Manually recreating the KElbowVisualizer look)
fig, ax1 = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))

# Plot Distortion Score (Teal)
ax1.plot(clusters, distortions, 'D-', color='teal', label='distortion score')
ax1.set_xlabel('Number of Clusters (k)')
ax1.set_ylabel('Distortion Score')
ax1.set_title('KMeans Elbow Plot: Finding the Optimal k', fontsize=14)
ax1.grid(True, linestyle='--', alpha=0.6)

# Plot Fit Time (Orange) on a twin axis
ax2 = ax1.twinx()
ax2.plot(clusters, fit_times, 'o--', color='orange', alpha=0.5, label='fit time')
ax2.set_ylabel('Fit Time (seconds)')

# Add a vertical line at the 'elbow' (k=4)
plt.axvline(x=4, color='red', linestyle='--', label='elbow at k=4')

# Combine legends from both axes
lines, labels = ax1.get_legend_handles_labels()
lines2, labels2 = ax2.get_legend_handles_labels()
ax1.legend(lines + lines2, labels + labels2, loc='upper right')

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Based on the Elbow Method and Average Distortion plots, the following observations can be made regarding the optimal number of clusters for this dataset:¶

Decreasing Distortion: As the number of clusters k increases, the average distortion — measured as the sum of squared distances from each data point to its assigned cluster center — decreases consistently, as expected. This reflects the fundamental principle that adding more clusters always reduces the within-cluster variance, since each additional center is able to capture a more granular subset of the data.¶
Initial Significant Drops: The most pronounced reductions in distortion occur as k moves from 1 to 4, indicating that transitioning from a single group to four distinct clusters captures a substantial portion of the data's underlying structure. Each additional cluster in this range contributes meaningfully to reducing the average distance between data points and their assigned centers, confirming that the data contains at least four genuinely distinct groupings.¶
Identifying the Elbow: The distortion curve begins to level off noticeably after k = 4, with a secondary inflection point observable around k = 7. These two values represent the most defensible elbow points in the curve — the stages at which the marginal benefit of adding an additional cluster diminishes most clearly relative to the preceding reductions.¶
Risk of Over-Clustering: While distortion continues to decrease as k increases beyond 7, selecting a very high value of k — such as 12 or 14 — risks over-clustering, whereby groups become too small, too granular, or too difficult to interpret meaningfully in the context of financial stock analysis. In such cases, the additional clusters may reflect noise or minor variations rather than genuinely distinct financial archetypes.¶
Recommended Number of Clusters: Based on the Elbow Method analysis, two values of k emerge as strong candidates: k = 4 is recommended for broad segmentation, providing a high-level classification of stocks into a small number of meaningful financial archetypes — such as Value, Growth, Risk, and Mega-Cap profiles — that are both interpretable and actionable for financial analysis. k = 7 may be more appropriate if a more granular breakdown of niche stock behaviors is desired, offering additional differentiation within the broader groupings identified at k = 4 without crossing into the territory of over-clustering.¶

    sil_score.append(score)
    print("For n_clusters = {}, the silhouette score is {})".format(n_clusters, score))

plt.plot(cluster_list, sil_score)
plt.show()

Based on the Silhouette Score analysis, the following observations can be made regarding the optimal number of clusters for this dataset:¶

Silhouette Score Rankings: The highest silhouette score is achieved with k = 2 (0.453), followed by k = 5 (0.438) and k = 4 (0.425). These three values of k produce the most well-defined and internally cohesive cluster structures according to this metric, with the remaining values of k recording comparatively lower scores.¶
Divergence from the Elbow Method: It is noteworthy that the Elbow Method previously suggested k = 4 or k = 7 as the most defensible cluster counts, while the Silhouette Score analysis points toward k = 2 or k = 5. This divergence highlights the inherently subjective nature of determining the optimal number of clusters and reinforces the importance of evaluating multiple complementary metrics before arriving at a final decision — no single method should be treated as definitive in isolation.¶
Why k = 2 is Statistically Optimal but Analytically Insufficient: While k = 2 technically achieves the highest silhouette score, it produces an overly simplistic segmentation that offers limited practical value for financial analysis. A two-cluster solution effectively reduces all stocks to a binary classification — broadly normal versus broadly unusual — and fails to capture the nuanced investment archetypes that make clustering a meaningful tool for portfolio analysis and stock categorization.¶
Why k = 5 is the Most Appropriate Final Choice: Despite a marginally lower silhouette score than k = 2, k = 5 represents the optimal balance between statistical validity and actionable financial insight for the following reasons:¶
Information Density: At k = 5, the largest cluster — the Market Core — is exceptionally well-defined, while the smaller clusters represent distinct and meaningful market niches that k = 2 would entirely obscure. A greater number of clusters crossing the average silhouette score threshold in the plot further supports the structural coherence of this solution.¶
Actionable Investment Archetypes: A five-cluster solution enables stocks to be categorized into clear and interpretable investment profiles — such as Growth, Value, Blue Chip, High-Risk, and Mega-Cap — providing a far richer and more actionable framework for financial decision-making than a two-cluster solution could offer.¶
Structural Stability: A silhouette score of 0.4381 is highly respectable for high-dimensional financial data, where clean cluster boundaries are inherently difficult to achieve. This score confirms that the five identified groups are sufficiently well-separated to be considered reliable and meaningful for practical investment analysis and decision-making.¶

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import time
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score

# Range of k to evaluate
k_range = range(2, 16)
silhouette_scores = []
fit_times = []

# Manual silhouette score and fit time calculation
for k in k_range:
    model = KMeans(n_clusters=k, n_init=10, random_state=1)
    
    # Measure fit time
    start = time.time()
    labels = model.fit_predict(k_means_df)
    end = time.time()
    
    # Measure silhouette score
    score = silhouette_score(k_means_df, labels)
    
    silhouette_scores.append(score)
    fit_times.append(end - start)

# Visualization of the results
fig, ax1 = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))

# Primary axis for Silhouette Score
ax1.plot(k_range, silhouette_scores, 'D-', color='teal', label='silhouette score')
ax1.set_xlabel('k')
ax1.set_ylabel('silhouette score')
ax1.set_title('Silhouette Score Elbow for KMeans Clustering (Manual)', fontsize=14)
ax1.grid(True, linestyle='--', alpha=0.6)

# Secondary axis for Fit Time
ax2 = ax1.twinx()
ax2.plot(k_range, fit_times, 'o--', color='orange', alpha=0.5, label='fit time')
ax2.set_ylabel('fit time (seconds)')

# Consolidate legends from both axes
lines1, labels1 = ax1.get_legend_handles_labels()
lines2, labels2 = ax2.get_legend_handles_labels()
ax1.legend(lines1 + lines2, labels1 + labels2, loc='upper right')

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.cm as cm
import numpy as np
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_samples, silhouette_score
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans

# 1. Setup the Model
n_clusters = 5
model = KMeans(n_clusters=n_clusters, n_init=10, random_state=1)
cluster_labels = model.fit_predict(k_means_df)
silhouette_avg = silhouette_score(k_means_df, cluster_labels)
sample_silhouette_values = silhouette_samples(k_means_df, cluster_labels)

# 2. Create the Visualization
fig, ax1 = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 7))
y_lower = 10

for i in range(n_clusters):
    # Aggregate and sort silhouette scores for this specific cluster
    ith_cluster_silhouette_values = sample_silhouette_values[cluster_labels == i]
    ith_cluster_silhouette_values.sort()

    size_cluster_i = ith_cluster_silhouette_values.shape[0]
    y_upper = y_lower + size_cluster_i

    # Color mapping
    color = cm.nipy_spectral(float(i) / n_clusters)
    ax1.fill_betweenx(np.arange(y_lower, y_upper), 0, ith_cluster_silhouette_values,
                      facecolor=color, edgecolor=color, alpha=0.7)

    # Label the cluster plots with their numbers
    ax1.text(-0.05, y_lower + 0.5 * size_cluster_i, str(i))

    # Compute the new y_lower for next plot
    y_lower = y_upper + 10 

# Formatting the plot
ax1.set_title("Silhouette Profile for k=5")
ax1.set_xlabel("Silhouette Coefficient Values")
ax1.set_ylabel("Cluster Label")

# Add a vertical line for the average silhouette score
ax1.axvline(x=silhouette_avg, color="red", linestyle="--")
ax1.set_yticks([])  # Clear the yaxis labels
ax1.set_xticks([-0.1, 0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8, 1])

plt.show()

Based on the Silhouette Profile for k = 5, the following observations can be made regarding the quality and structure of the clustering solution:¶

Overall Silhouette Score: The average silhouette score for k = 5 is approximately 0.4317, represented by the red dashed line in the profile plot. This score is moderate but robust for high-dimensional financial data, indicating a reasonable and reliable degree of separation among the five clusters — confirming that stocks are, on the whole, meaningfully more similar to members of their own cluster than to those in neighboring clusters.¶
Cluster 0 — The Market Core (Well-Defined): Cluster 0 is by far the largest and most cohesive cluster in the solution, with the vast majority of its data points recording silhouette coefficients well above the average line. This exceptionally strong internal cohesion confirms that the Market Core represents a genuinely distinct and tightly grouped segment of stocks — the dominant archetype within the dataset — whose members are clearly and consistently separated from all other clusters.¶
Cluster 4 — Strong Definition: Cluster 4 also performs well in the silhouette profile, with a considerable proportion of its data points extending beyond the average silhouette score. This indicates that the stocks assigned to this cluster are well-separated from neighboring clusters and form a reasonably compact and internally consistent group.¶
Clusters 1, 2, and 3 — Specialized but Boundary-Adjacent: Clusters 1, 2, and 3 represent the more specialized niche groups in the solution — such as Mega-Cap Titans and Distressed stocks — and while smaller in size, their overall silhouette shapes are broadly consistent. However, a subset of data points in each of these clusters dip toward or below zero, indicating that some stocks in these groups sit closer to the boundaries of neighboring clusters than to the core of their own assigned cluster. The presence of negative silhouette coefficients in these clusters suggests a degree of overlap between adjacent cluster boundaries, and implies that a small number of data points may be more accurately assigned to a different cluster.¶
Cluster Size and Density: The vertical extent of each section in the silhouette plot reflects the number of samples assigned to that cluster, while the horizontal spread reflects the internal homogeneity of the group. Clusters with narrower but consistently positive silhouette values — such as Cluster 0 and Cluster 4 — are generally better defined, while the wider spread and mixed coefficient signs observed in Clusters 1, 2, and 3 indicate greater internal heterogeneity and less clearly demarcated boundaries.¶
Overlap and Potential Misclassification: The negative silhouette coefficients observed in Clusters 1, 2, and 3 indicate that a portion of data points in these groups may be poorly clustered — either sitting at the margins between two clusters or potentially belonging more naturally to a neighboring group. In an ideal clustering solution, all silhouette coefficients would be positive and approach 1.0; the presence of negative values serves as a signal that these boundary regions warrant further investigation, and that future iterations of the model may benefit from feature refinement or alternative clustering approaches to sharpen the boundaries of these niche clusters.¶
Overall: The Silhouette Profile for k = 5 presents a mixed but broadly positive picture. The solution is anchored by a dominant and exceptionally well-defined Market Core cluster, complemented by a strong Cluster 4, while the three remaining specialized clusters exhibit varying degrees of boundary overlap and internal heterogeneity. This variability is not uncommon in high-dimensional financial datasets, where niche stock profiles naturally resist clean separation. The overall silhouette score of 0.4317 confirms that the five-cluster solution is structurally sound and suitable for practical financial analysis, while the boundary overlap in the smaller clusters highlights areas where further model refinement could yield incremental improvements.¶

init init: {'k-means++', 'random'}, callable or array-like of shape (n_clusters, n_features), default='k-means++'

Method for initialization:

* 'k-means++' : selects initial cluster centroids using sampling based on an empirical probability distribution of the points' contribution to the overall inertia. This technique speeds up convergence. The algorithm implemented is "greedy k-means++". It differs from the vanilla k-means++ by making several trials at each sampling step and choosing the best centroid among them.

* 'random': choose `n_clusters` observations (rows) at random from data for the initial centroids.

* If an array is passed, it should be of shape (n_clusters, n_features) and gives the initial centers.

* If a callable is passed, it should take arguments X, n_clusters and a random state and return an initialization.

For an example of how to use the different `init` strategies, see
:ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_cluster_plot_kmeans_digits.py`.

n_init n_init: 'auto' or int, default='auto'

Number of times the k-means algorithm is run with different centroid
seeds. The final results is the best output of `n_init` consecutive runs
in terms of inertia. Several runs are recommended for sparse
high-dimensional problems (see :ref:`kmeans_sparse_high_dim`).

When `n_init='auto'`, the number of runs depends on the value of init:
10 if using `init='random'` or `init` is a callable;
1 if using `init='k-means++'` or `init` is an array-like.

Based on the K-Means cluster profile analysis, the following observations can be made regarding the five identified segments and their distinguishing financial characteristics:¶

Cluster 0 — The Balanced Performers (139 companies): This is the largest cluster in the solution, representing the broadest and most representative cross-section of stocks in the dataset. With a moderate current price of approximately $73.64, moderate volatility of 1.40, and broadly positive net cash flow, net income, and EPS figures, these companies reflect the baseline behavior of the typical stock in the dataset. The moderate P/E ratio of approximately 23.72 and ROE of 25.07 further confirm their broadly average valuation and profitability profiles. The negative P/B ratio of approximately -2.64 warrants attention, suggesting that some companies in this cluster may carry accumulated losses or have book values below their market values — a nuance worth investigating further. Overall, this cluster serves as the market core reference point against which the more specialized clusters can be meaningfully compared.¶
Cluster 1 — The High-Volatility Underperformers (31 companies): This cluster is defined by the highest average volatility across all five segments (2.77), a significantly negative average price change of approximately -11.76%, and negative net income of approximately -$2.1 billion and EPS of approximately -5.39 — collectively painting a picture of high-risk, loss-making companies with poor recent price performance. The very high P/E ratio of approximately 96.95 is likely a distortion caused by negative or near-zero earnings rather than genuine growth expectations, and should be interpreted with caution. The moderate positive ROE of approximately 48.19 appears counterintuitive given the negative income figures, and may reflect the influence of specific financial structures or a small number of high-ROE companies within the cluster skewing the average upward. These stocks represent a high-risk investment profile with limited near-term return potential based on current fundamentals.¶
Cluster 2 — The High-Price Premium Growth Stocks (8 companies): Despite being the smallest cluster alongside Cluster 3, this group is among the most distinctive in the dataset, characterized by a very high average current price of approximately $525.42 — significantly above all other clusters — and an extremely high P/E ratio of approximately 113.90 and P/B ratio of approximately 30.23. These metrics collectively indicate that the market assigns a substantial premium to these stocks relative to their current earnings and book value, reflecting strong investor expectations for future growth. The very high average cash ratio of approximately 259.00 further distinguishes this cluster, suggesting that these companies maintain exceptionally strong liquidity positions. Positive net cash flow, net income, and EPS figures confirm that, unlike Clusters 1 and 3, these are profitable companies whose high valuations are supported by genuine financial strength rather than speculative interest alone.¶
Cluster 3 — The Distressed High-Risk Companies (7 companies): This cluster represents the most concerning risk profile in the dataset, characterized by significantly negative net cash flow, net income, and EPS — with average net income reaching approximately -$4.9 billion — alongside the lowest average cash ratio of approximately 33.57 and the most deeply negative P/B ratio of approximately -11.59. The exceptionally high average ROE of approximately 633.57 is almost certainly a distortion caused by highly negative or near-zero equity bases rather than genuine operational efficiency, and serves as a red flag rather than a positive signal. The combination of massive financial losses, deeply negative book equity, and elevated volatility of approximately 1.83 identifies these companies as severely financially distressed, with some possible speculative investor interest reflected in the moderate P/E ratio of approximately 42.28. These stocks represent the highest-risk segment in the dataset and warrant extreme caution from an investment perspective.¶
Cluster 4 — The Value Titans / Large-Cap Low P/E Stocks (13 companies): This cluster stands out as the most attractive from a value investing perspective, recording the highest average net income ($14.1 billion), the lowest average P/E ratio (16.10), and the lowest average volatility (1.16) across all five segments. The extremely high average estimated shares outstanding of approximately 3.9 billion confirms that these are mega-cap corporations operating at a scale far beyond the typical company in the dataset. Despite their exceptional profitability and financial strength — evidenced by the strongest positive net cash flow, net income, and EPS figures in the dataset — these companies trade at the most conservative earnings multiples, suggesting they may be undervalued relative to their earnings power or represent mature, stable businesses that the market prices with low growth premiums. The negative P/B ratio of approximately -4.25, while noteworthy, is consistent with companies that have engaged in significant share buyback programmes or carry accounting structures that reduce book equity below zero without reflecting financial distress.¶

Volatility → Cluster 1 (~2.77): The High-Volatility Underperformers carry the highest average risk profile.¶

Cluster 0 — The Balanced Performers (281 companies): The largest segment by a considerable margin, Cluster 0 represents the broad market baseline. These companies exhibit moderate current prices, moderate volatility, positive but average price changes, and generally profitable financials across net cash flow, net income, and EPS. Their moderate P/E ratio of approximately 23.72 reflects conventional market valuations, while the negative P/B ratio of approximately -2.64 suggests that some companies in this group may carry accumulated losses or hold book values below their market values. As the dominant cluster, this segment provides the most representative picture of typical stock behavior in the dataset and serves as the natural reference point for interpreting the more specialized clusters.¶
Cluster 1 — The High-Volatility Underperformers (31 companies): This segment is defined by the highest average volatility across all clusters (2.77), a significantly negative average price change of approximately -11.76%, and negative net income and EPS — collectively identifying these as high-risk, loss-making companies with poor recent price performance. The very high P/E ratio of approximately 96.95 is a distortion driven by negative or near-zero earnings rather than genuine growth expectations. The moderately positive ROE of approximately 48.19 appears counterintuitive in the context of negative income and likely reflects the influence of specific financial structures or a small number of outliers within the cluster. These stocks represent the highest-risk, lowest near-term return profile among all segments, and are best approached with considerable caution.¶
Cluster 2 — The High-Priced Premium Growth Stocks (8 companies): This small but highly distinctive segment is characterized by the highest average current price of approximately $525.42, very high P/E (113.90) and P/B (30.23) ratios, and a very high average cash ratio of approximately 259.00 — reflecting exceptional liquidity. Positive and strong net cash flow, net income, and EPS figures confirm that these are genuinely profitable companies whose premium valuations are underpinned by real financial strength and strong investor expectations for future growth, rather than speculative interest alone. These stocks are likely to appeal to growth-oriented investors willing to pay a significant premium for quality and future potential.¶
Cluster 3 — The Distressed High-Risk Companies (7 companies): This segment presents the most complex and cautionary risk profile in the dataset. The exceptionally high average ROE of approximately 633.57 is almost certainly an accounting artifact driven by deeply negative book equity rather than genuine operational efficiency, and should be interpreted as a warning signal rather than a positive indicator. This assessment is reinforced by the significantly negative net cash flow, net income, and EPS figures, the most deeply negative P/B ratio of approximately -11.59, and the lowest average cash ratio of approximately 33.57 across all segments. The combination of massive financial losses, negative equity, and above-average volatility identifies these companies as severely financially distressed. Any residual market interest in these stocks likely reflects speculative positioning rather than fundamental investment merit.¶
Cluster 4 — The Value Titans / Large-Cap Low P/E Stocks (13 companies): This segment stands out as the most compelling from a value investing perspective, recording the highest average net income of approximately $14.11 billion, the lowest average P/E ratio of 16.10, and the lowest average volatility of 1.16 across all five clusters. The extremely high average estimated shares outstanding of approximately 3.9 billion confirms their mega-cap status. Despite exceptional profitability and financial stability, these companies trade at conservative earnings multiples — suggesting they may be undervalued relative to their earnings power or represent mature, large-scale businesses that the market prices with modest growth premiums. The negative P/B ratio of approximately -4.25 is consistent with significant share buyback activity or accounting structures that reduce book equity without reflecting financial distress. These stocks are ideally suited to value-oriented, risk-averse investors seeking stable returns from financially robust, large-cap companies.¶

The presence of Energy and Consumer Staples, combined with its financial profile, suggests that these may represent distressed cases within those sectors.¶

The strong presence of Financials and Telecommunications is consistent with the profile of large, mature, and potentially undervalued firms.¶

Based on the boxplots of numerical variables across each K-Means cluster, the following observations can be made regarding the visual confirmation of each segment's distinct financial characteristics:¶

Feature-Level Observations:¶

Current Price: Cluster 2 (Elite Premium) stands out unambiguously, with a significantly higher price range than all other clusters — visually confirming its status as the high-valuation segment. The remaining four clusters are concentrated at considerably lower price points, with their distributions largely overlapping relative to the scale established by Cluster 2's elevated range.¶
Price Change: Cluster 1 (High-Volatility Underperformers) displays a distribution centered distinctly below zero, providing clear visual confirmation of its underperformer profile. All other clusters record distributions primarily above zero, reinforcing the conclusion that Cluster 1's negative price performance is a segment-specific characteristic rather than a broader market trend.¶
Volatility: Cluster 1 exhibits the highest and widest volatility distribution across all segments, with both a higher median and a broader interquartile range — confirming its high-risk profile. Cluster 4 (Value Titans), at the other extreme, records the lowest and most tightly concentrated volatility distribution, visually affirming its characterization as the most stable and risk-averse segment.¶
ROE: Cluster 3 (Distressed High-Risk) displays an exceptionally high and widely spread ROE distribution that sits far above all other clusters. As established in the earlier cluster profile analysis, this extreme ROE is not indicative of genuine operational efficiency but rather reflects a distortion caused by deeply negative book equity. All other clusters record considerably more moderate and compact ROE distributions, further highlighting Cluster 3 as a statistical outlier in this metric.¶
Cash Ratio: Cluster 2 records the highest cash ratio distribution by a significant margin, visually confirming its exceptionally strong liquidity position. Cluster 3, at the opposite extreme, displays the lowest cash ratio distribution — consistent with its financially distressed profile and limited capacity to meet short-term obligations.¶
Net Cash Flow, Net Income, and Earnings Per Share: Cluster 4 (Value Titans / Mega-Cap Titans) consistently records the highest positive values across all three profitability metrics, with its distributions positioned clearly above those of all other clusters — confirming that these companies operate in a profitability league of their own. Clusters 1 and 3, conversely, display significant negative values across these same metrics, with notable downside outliers in EPS for both segments, visually separating the loss-making companies from the consistently profitable ones.¶
Estimated Shares Outstanding: Cluster 4 dominates this metric by an extraordinary margin, with its distribution positioned far above all other clusters. This visual confirmation reinforces the mega-cap nature of this segment — these are not merely profitable companies but structurally massive corporations whose scale of operations is categorically different from the rest of the dataset.¶
P/E and P/B Ratios: Cluster 2 records the highest P/E and P/B ratio distributions, visually confirming its premium growth valuation profile and strong market-to-book premium. Cluster 4 records the lowest P/E distribution, consistent with its characterization as a potentially undervalued large-cap segment. Notably, Clusters 0, 3, and 4 all display negative P/B ratio distributions, with Cluster 3 recording the most deeply negative values — highlighting the unusual and distressed book value situations present in these segments.¶

Insights¶

Key Insights and Strategic Conclusions from the K-Means Clustering Analysis¶

Data Quality and Preprocessing: The dataset provides a clean and reliable foundation for analysis, with no missing values or duplicate entries identified during preprocessing. However, the near-universal presence of significant outliers and heavy right-skewness across most numerical features — including Current Price, ROE, Cash Ratio, Net Income, P/E Ratio, P/B Ratio, and Estimated Shares Outstanding — reflects the high degree of financial heterogeneity inherent in stock market data. While the data was appropriately scaled prior to clustering, further specialized outlier treatment — such as winsorization or feature-specific log transformation — may be worth considering in future iterations to improve the robustness of the clustering boundaries, particularly for the smaller and more boundary-adjacent segments.¶

The exploratory data analysis revealed meaningful variation in financial performance across GICS sectors, with the following key patterns:¶

Health Care recorded the highest average price increase and among the strongest cash ratio figures, reflecting sustained investor confidence and strong liquidity across the sector.¶
Energy was the only sector to record a negative average price change, alongside the highest average volatility — findings that are directly confirmed by the clustering analysis, where Energy stocks account for approximately 71% of Cluster 1's membership.¶
Information Technology recorded the highest average P/E ratio, consistent with strong market expectations for future earnings growth.¶
Utilities and Consumer Staples exhibited the lowest average volatility, reinforcing their reputations as defensive, income-oriented sectors that provide portfolio stability.¶
The correlation analysis identified several notable relationships among the financial metrics:¶
Strong positive correlations were observed among profitability metrics — Net Cash Flow, Net Income, and Earnings Per Share — confirming that these variables move in a broadly consistent direction across the dataset.¶
ROE and P/B Ratio also showed a notable positive relationship, reflecting the intuitive link between equity efficiency and market-to-book valuation.¶
Volatility and Cash Ratio exhibited generally weak correlations with most other financial metrics, suggesting that these variables capture dimensions of risk and liquidity that are relatively independent of the profitability and valuation metrics in the dataset — and therefore contribute distinct and non-redundant information to the clustering model.¶

K-Means Cluster Profiles — Five Distinct Investment Archetypes¶

The five-cluster solution successfully identifies a meaningful and interpretable spectrum of market segments, structured as follows:¶
Cluster 0 — The Market Core / Balanced Performers (281 companies — 82.6% of dataset): The dominant segment, representing the standard performance benchmark for the index. With an average price of $73.64, moderate volatility of 1.40, and broadly positive profitability metrics, these companies account for approximately 81.7% of the total net income in the sample. Their broad sectoral diversity — led by Industrials, Financials, Consumer Discretionary, and Health Care — reinforces their role as the stable foundation of the market. The negative average P/B ratio warrants monitoring but does not detract from the segment's overall financial health.¶
Cluster 1 — The High-Volatility Underperformers / Speculative Growth (31 companies): Predominantly driven by Energy sector stocks (22 of 31 companies), this segment is characterized by the highest average volatility (2.77), a significantly negative average price change of approximately -11.76%, and average net losses of approximately -$2.1 billion. These are high-risk, underperforming assets that represent a net drag on total market earnings, and should be approached with considerable caution by risk-averse investors.¶
Cluster 2 — The Elite Premium Growth Stocks (8 companies): A small but highly distinctive segment defined by the highest average share price ($525.42), an extreme average P/E ratio of 113.90, and an exceptionally high average cash ratio of 259.00. Drawing from Consumer Discretionary, Health Care, Information Technology, and Real Estate, these stocks — which include prominent names such as Amazon and Facebook — are valued primarily on the basis of future growth expectations rather than current earnings. They represent compelling opportunities for growth-oriented investors willing to pay a significant premium for quality and long-term potential.¶
Cluster 3 — The Distressed High-Risk / Value Traps (7 companies): The most complex and cautionary segment in the dataset. The exceptionally high average ROE of approximately 633.57 is an accounting artifact of deeply negative book equity rather than genuine operational efficiency, and is accompanied by the most severely negative net income (-$4.9 billion average), the most deeply negative P/B ratio (-11.59), and the lowest cash ratio (33.57) across all segments. These companies exhibit the hallmarks of severe financial distress and represent potential value traps — stocks that may superficially appear efficient due to distorted financial ratios but carry substantial fundamental risk. Extreme caution and thorough due diligence are essential before any investment consideration.¶
Cluster 4 — The Value Titans / Mega-Cap Low P/E Stocks (13 companies): Despite comprising only 13 companies, this segment generates over 36% of the total market profit in the dataset, with an average net income of approximately $14.1 billion. Characterized by the lowest average P/E ratio (16.10), the lowest average volatility (1.16), and the highest estimated shares outstanding (~3.9 billion), these large-cap companies — concentrated in Financials, Health Care, and Telecommunications Services — represent mature, highly profitable, and potentially undervalued investment opportunities ideally suited to value-oriented, risk-averse investors seeking stable long-term returns.¶

Hierarchical Clustering¶

Computing Cophenetic Correlation¶

hc_df = subset_scaled_df.copy()
In [105]:
# List of common distance metrics
distance_metrics = ['euclidean', 'cityblock', 'chebyshev']

# List of common linkage methods
linkage_methods = ['single', 'complete', 'average', 'ward']

high_cophenet_corr = 0
high_dm_lm = [0, 0]

for dm in distance_metrics:
    for lm in linkage_methods:
        # Note: 'ward' linkage only supports 'euclidean' distance in SciPy
        if lm == 'ward' and dm != 'euclidean':
            continue
        
        Z = linkage(hc_df, metric=dm, method=lm)
        c, coph_dists = cophenet(Z, pdist(hc_df, metric=dm))
        
        print(
            "Cophenetic correlation for {} distance and {} linkage is {}.".format(
                dm.capitalize(), lm, c
            )
        )
        if high_cophenet_corr < c:
            high_cophenet_corr = c
            high_dm_lm[0] = dm
            high_dm_lm[1] = lm

# Printing the results
print('*'*100)
print(
    "Highest cophenetic correlation is {}, which is obtained with {} distance and {} linkage.".format(
        high_cophenet_corr, high_dm_lm[0].capitalize(), high_dm_lm[1]
    )
)

    Z = linkage(hc_df, metric="euclidean", method=lm)
    c, coph_dists = cophenet(Z, pdist(hc_df, metric='euclidean'))

Based on the analysis of different linkage methods using Euclidean distance, the following observations can be made regarding their relative performance in preserving the original pairwise dissimilarities of the data:¶

Average Linkage — Best Performing (Cophenetic Correlation: 0.9422): The average linkage method achieves the highest cophenetic correlation of approximately 0.9422, making it the most reliable and appropriate choice for hierarchical clustering of this stock dataset when using Euclidean distance. This high correlation confirms that the dendrogram produced by average linkage most faithfully preserves the original pairwise distances between data points, meaning that the hierarchical structure it generates is a highly accurate representation of the underlying data relationships.¶
Single Linkage — Strong Performance (Cophenetic Correlation: 0.9232): Single linkage also performs strongly, recording a cophenetic correlation of approximately 0.9232 — the second highest among all methods evaluated. While marginally below average linkage, this remains a high and reliable score, indicating that single linkage also produces a dendrogram that closely reflects the original pairwise dissimilarities. However, single linkage is known to be susceptible to the chaining effect — where clusters are linked through a series of close individual points rather than overall cluster similarity — which may limit its practical utility for producing well-defined and compact cluster groupings in financial data.¶
Complete Linkage — Moderate Performance (Cophenetic Correlation: 0.7873): Complete linkage records a notably lower cophenetic correlation of approximately 0.7873, indicating a moderate degree of distortion in its dendrogram representation of the original data structure. While complete linkage tends to produce more compact and evenly sized clusters than single linkage, its reduced ability to faithfully preserve pairwise distances in this dataset makes it a less suitable choice than average or single linkage for this specific application.¶
Ward Linkage — Weakest Performance (Cophenetic Correlation: 0.7101): Ward linkage records the lowest cophenetic correlation of approximately 0.7101 — the weakest result among all four methods evaluated. Despite its widespread popularity in clustering applications due to its tendency to produce evenly sized and internally compact clusters, Ward linkage introduces the most significant distortion into the hierarchical structure of this dataset. This is likely attributable to the fact that Ward linkage performs optimally when the underlying data clusters are roughly spherical and similarly sized — conditions that are not consistently met in this high-dimensional, heavily skewed financial dataset.¶
Overall: The cophenetic correlation analysis provides clear and consistent guidance on the most appropriate linkage method for hierarchical clustering of this dataset. Average linkage emerges as the definitive best choice, offering the highest fidelity representation of the original pairwise data structure with a cophenetic correlation of 0.9422. The ranking of all four methods is summarized below:¶

Let's view the dendrograms for the different linkage methods with Euclidean distance.¶

Checking Dendrograms¶

In [107]:
# list of linkage methods
linkage_methods = ['single', 'complete', 'average', 'centroid', 'ward', 'weighted'] 

# lists to save results of cophenetic correlation calculation
compare_cols = ["Linkage", "Cophenetic Coefficient"]
compare = []

# to create a subplot image
fig, axs = plt.subplots(len(linkage_methods), 1, figsize=(15, 30))

# Enumerate through the list of linkage methods
for i, method in enumerate(linkage_methods):
    Z = linkage(hc_df, metric="euclidean", method=method)

    # Plotting truncated dendrogram for readability
    dendrogram(Z, ax=axs[i], truncate_mode='lastp', p=30)
    axs[i].set_title(f"Dendrogram ({method.capitalize()} Linkage)")

    # Calculate cophenetic correlation
    coph_corr, coph_dist = cophenet(Z, pdist(hc_df))
    axs[i].annotate(
        f"Cophenetic\nCorrelation\n{coph_corr:0.2f}",
        (0.80, 0.80),
        xycoords="axes fraction",
        bbox=dict(boxstyle="round", fc="w")
    )

    compare.append([method, coph_corr])

Based on the comparison of linkage methods and the interpretation of the resulting dendrograms, the following observations can be made:¶

Linkage Method Performance Comparison¶
The cophenetic correlation measures how faithfully each linkage method preserves the original pairwise distances between stocks in the dendrogram structure. The four methods rank as follows:¶
Average Linkage (0.94) — Best Performer: Average linkage achieves the highest cophenetic correlation, confirming it as the most accurate method for preserving the true pairwise distances between stocks in this dataset. By computing the average distance between all members of two clusters before merging them, this method effectively balances sensitivity to outliers — successfully isolating distinct groups such as the Mega-Cap Titans — without introducing significant distortion to the broader structure of the main stock population.¶
Centroid Linkage (0.93) — Strong Runner-Up: Centroid linkage performs closely behind average linkage, focusing on the geometric center of each cluster as the basis for distance computation. While its cophenetic correlation of 0.93 confirms strong distance preservation, it is marginally less reliable than average linkage and can occasionally produce inversions in the dendrogram — where a merger appears at a lower height than a previous one — which can complicate interpretation.¶
Single Linkage (0.92) — Strong but Prone to Chaining: Single linkage also records a high cophenetic correlation of 0.92, indicating strong overall distance preservation. However, the dendrograms produced by this method frequently exhibit a pronounced chaining effect — where the algorithm progressively picks off individual outlier stocks one by one rather than forming cohesive, well-defined groups. This behavior can make single linkage dendrograms visually difficult to interpret and less suitable for identifying meaningful cluster boundaries in financial data.¶
Ward Linkage (0.71) — Weakest Performer: Despite producing the most visually balanced and evenly sized clusters — making it a popular choice for general-purpose clustering applications — Ward linkage records the lowest cophenetic correlation of 0.71, indicating the highest degree of distortion relative to the original pairwise distances. This suggests that Ward linkage is not well-suited to preserving the true hierarchical structure of this specific stock dataset, likely because the underlying data does not conform to the spherical, similarly sized cluster geometry that Ward linkage implicitly assumes.¶
Cophenetic Correlation and Dendrogram Fidelity: The average linkage method with Euclidean distance yields the highest cophenetic correlation of approximately 0.94, confirming that its dendrogram is the most faithful visual representation of the actual distances between data points. This makes it the most reliable basis for identifying the hierarchical structure of the stock dataset.¶
Overall: The combined quantitative and visual analysis of linkage methods consistently identifies average linkage with Euclidean distance as the optimal configuration for hierarchical clustering of this stock dataset. Its cophenetic correlation of 0.94 provides strong statistical justification for its selection, while its balanced cluster formation behavior makes the resulting dendrogram the most reliable and interpretable basis for identifying the natural groupings within the data. A careful horizontal cut of the average linkage dendrogram — guided by the longest vertical gaps — will yield the most meaningful and well-supported cluster assignments for subsequent analysis.¶

Based on the hierarchical clustering analysis, the following final insights and key takeaways can be drawn regarding the comparative performance of the linkage methods evaluated:¶

Average Linkage is the Clear Winner (0.9422): The average linkage method achieves the highest cophenetic correlation of 0.9422, confirming it as the most accurate and reliable method for hierarchical clustering of this stock dataset. This high score indicates that the resulting dendrogram is an excellent and faithful representation of the actual pairwise distances between companies, preserving the true hierarchical relationships within the data with very high fidelity. For this reason, average linkage with Euclidean distance is the definitive recommended configuration for the hierarchical clustering of this dataset.¶
Strong Performance of Average, Centroid, and Single Linkage — A Signal of Natural Data Structure: The consistently high cophenetic correlations achieved by average (0.9422), centroid (0.93), and single (0.9232) linkage methods collectively suggest that this dataset possesses a strong and well-defined natural hierarchical structure. This is likely driven by the presence of distinct financial outliers — most notably the Mega-Cap Titans and Elite Premium stocks — whose extreme financial profiles create substantial pairwise distances from the market core, producing clearly demarcated groupings that multiple linkage methods are able to detect and preserve with high accuracy.¶
Single Linkage — Strong but Limited by Chaining (0.9232): Despite its high cophenetic correlation, single linkage is prone to the chaining effect — where the algorithm progressively absorbs individual outlier stocks one by one rather than forming cohesive cluster groups. While this behavior contributes to its strong distance-preservation score, it limits the practical interpretability of the resulting dendrogram for financial cluster analysis, making it a less preferable choice than average linkage despite its competitive correlation score.¶
Complete Linkage — Moderate Performance with Notable Distortion (0.7873): Complete linkage records a moderate cophenetic correlation of 0.7873, reflecting a meaningful degree of distortion relative to the original pairwise distances. While it tends to produce more compact and spherical clusters than single linkage, its sensitivity to outliers — which can cause premature merging of distantly related stocks — reduces its suitability for this dataset relative to the top-performing methods.¶
Ward Linkage — Popular but Least Suitable Here (0.7101): Ward linkage records the lowest cophenetic correlation of 0.7101, confirming that it introduces the highest degree of distortion into the true hierarchical relationships of the stocks in this dataset. While Ward linkage is widely used in practice due to its tendency to produce visually balanced and evenly sized clusters, this advantage comes at a significant cost in terms of distance fidelity for this specific financial dataset. The performance gap between Ward linkage (0.7101) and the top three methods (all above 0.92) is substantial and provides clear evidence that Ward linkage is not well-suited to the structure of this data — likely because the heavily skewed, outlier-rich financial metrics do not conform to the spherical, similarly sized cluster geometry that Ward linkage implicitly assumes.¶

Connectivity matrix. Defines for each sample the neighboring

Stop early the construction of the tree at ``n_clusters``. This is
useful to decrease computation time if the number of clusters is not
small compared to the number of samples. This option is useful only
when specifying a connectivity matrix. Note also that when varying the
number of clusters and using caching, it may be advantageous to compute
the full tree. It must be ``True`` if ``distance_threshold`` is not

Otherwise, "auto" is equivalent to `False`. 		'auto'
linkage linkage: {'ward', 'complete', 'average', 'single'}, default='ward'

Which linkage criterion to use. The linkage criterion determines which
distance to use between sets of observation. The algorithm will merge
the pairs of cluster that minimize this criterion.

- 'ward' minimizes the variance of the clusters being merged.
- 'average' uses the average of the distances of each observation of
the two sets.
- 'complete' or 'maximum' linkage uses the maximum distances between
all observations of the two sets.
- 'single' uses the minimum of the distances between all observations
of the two sets.
